section_title: How do the sailors respond when Jonah tells them to throw him overboard?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 11 Now the sea was growing worse and worse, so they said to Jonah, “What must we do to you to calm this sea for us?” 12 “Pick me up,” he answered, “and cast me into the sea, so it may quiet down for you. For I know that I am to blame for this violent storm that has come upon you.” 13 Nevertheless, the men rowed hard to get back to dry land, but they could not, for the sea was raging against them more and more.

14 So they cried out to the LORD: “Please, O LORD, do not let us perish on account of this man’s life! Do not charge us with innocent blood! For You, O LORD, have done as You pleased.” 15 Then they picked up Jonah and cast him into the sea, and the raging sea grew calm. 16 Then the men feared the LORD greatly, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows to Him.

context_lines: As the storm worsens, Jonah tells the sailors to throw him into the sea, acknowledging that it has come because of him.
They first try to row back to dry land. When that fails, they call on the Lord, asking not to be charged with innocent blood. Only then do they throw Jonah overboard, and the sea becomes calm.

The sailors respond with great fear of the Lord, sacrifice and vows. Their concern to spare Jonah’s life stands beside his earlier unwillingness to carry God’s warning to Nineveh. People initially praying to different gods are now calling on the Lord and honoring Him.
common_interpretation_lines: [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jonah/1.htm) understands Jonah’s admission as accepting responsibility and punishment. [Wesley](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/jonah/1.htm) emphasizes the sailors’ efforts to save him and their later acknowledgment of the Lord. The text gives Jonah’s words, without explaining everything he hoped would happen to himself.
god_plan_lines: A strong parallel appears in [Mark 4:35–41](https://biblehub.com/bsb/mark/4.htm): a storm, a sleeping figure, terrified companions and sudden calm, followed by deep fear at the power revealed.

The difference brings Jesus into focus. Jonah’s disobedience has endangered the ship; Jesus commands the wind and sea Himself. The disciples are left asking who He is, that creation obeys Him. Read together, the accounts direct attention to God’s rule over the sea and the authority revealed in His Son.
